passage: I am Salma, and at twenty I was not trained for anything when a scooter skidded on the bridge road in front of me. The rider lay still. My legs shook. Everyone said, "Lift him, put him in an auto!" I said no. I switched on my hazard lights, put my scooter across the lane, and asked Jahnavi, my classmate who was on the pillion, to wave the traffic back. I called 112 and did what the operator said, one thing at a time. I stayed near the rider and kept telling him help was coming. Not moving him was the hardest part, because everyone wanted to.

qa.q: Where did the scooter skid?
qa.a: The scooter skidded on the bridge road.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling as the rider lay still?
qa.a: Salma was scared, with shaking legs, but chose calm steps instead of panicking.

qa.q: What was the key choice Salma made when others said to lift the rider?
qa.a: Salma refused to lift him, kept the scene safe, called 112 and followed the operator's instructions.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have felt when asked to wave the traffic back?
qa.a: Jahnavi may have felt nervous but useful, since standing in the road to slow the traffic was a clear task in the middle of a frightening moment.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling an untrained person keeping a scene safe, calling emergency services, staying with the injured and not moving the rider.

passage: The stairwell light was off because of a power cut, and Irawati's phone was at four percent. A thud sounded from the landing below. She found Salma aunty on the floor, holding her ankle, and two neighbours already reaching to pull her up. "Please don't lift her," Irawati said. Her voice shook, but she held her phone torch steady and dialled 112 while the screen still glowed. The operator gave simple instructions, and Irawati repeated them to the neighbours. When the battery died, she borrowed a neighbour's phone to keep the line open. She sat on the step, held Salma aunty's hand and said, "They are on their way."

qa.q: What percent was Irawati's phone at?
qa.a: Irawati's phone was at four percent.

qa.q: What is Irawati feeling as she says "Please don't lift her"?
qa.a: Irawati is scared, since her voice shakes, but she holds the torch steady and speaks up anyway.

qa.q: What choices helped when the phone battery died?
qa.a: Irawati borrowed a neighbour's phone to keep the line open and kept following the operator's instructions.

qa.q: What might Salma aunty need most from the people around her on the landing?
qa.a: Salma aunty probably needs calm company, being told that help is on the way, and not being pulled up while she is hurt.

grounding: Shows an untrained scared person keeping a scene safe, calling emergency services, staying with the injured and following the operator's instructions.

passage: On a rainy night in Chennai, Mohit, nineteen, and his friend Amandeep were walking home when a scooter skidded ahead of them. The rider lay on the road, groaning, one leg bent oddly. Mohit had never done first aid. His legs felt like water. But he stepped into the road and waved his phone torch at the traffic while Amandeep dialled 112. "Don't lift him," the operator said. "Is he breathing? Keep him still and talk to him." Mohit knelt beside the rider and kept him from trying to sit up. "Help is coming. What's your name?" He repeated the operator's questions aloud to Amandeep. The ambulance came. Mohit's hands shook for an hour afterwards.

qa.q: What did Mohit use to warn the traffic?
qa.a: He waved his phone torch at the traffic.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel when he saw the rider on the road?
qa.a: He felt terrified, his legs like water, since he had never done first aid.

qa.q: What did Mohit and Amandeep do right, even without training?
qa.a: They made the scene safe, called 112, followed the operator's instructions, kept the rider still and stayed with him until the ambulance came.

qa.q: How might the rider have felt with Mohit talking to him?
qa.a: The rider, in pain and frightened, likely felt a little calmer with someone beside him saying help was coming.

grounding: Shows an untrained young man keeping a road accident scene safe, calling emergency services and following the operator while not moving the injured rider.

passage:
Anjali: "Jeevan! Your neighbour's on the stairs, he's not moving!"
Jeevan: "Uncle! Uncle, can you hear me?"
(A faint groan.)
Anjali: "Should we carry him to the flat?"
Jeevan: "No. I don't know first aid, but don't move him. I'll call 112."
Anjali: "What do I do?"
Jeevan: "Go and tell the building guard to open the gate for the ambulance."
(Jeevan on the phone.)
Jeevan: "Building C, Green Park Society, third floor stairs. He fell. He's breathing. Okay... okay. Keep him still, don't give water."
Anjali: (returning) "Guard's at the gate."
Jeevan: (kneeling) "Uncle, the ambulance is coming. I'm right here."
(Jeevan stays beside him, holding the phone to his ear, until the paramedics arrive.)

qa.q: Where did the neighbour fall?
qa.a: On the third floor stairs of Building C, Green Park Society.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling on seeing the neighbour?
qa.a: Anjali felt alarmed and scared, shouting for Jeevan and wanting to carry him.

qa.q: Which things did Jeevan do right despite having no training?
qa.a: Jeevan didn't move the neighbour, called 112, sent Anjali to guide the ambulance, followed the operator's instructions and stayed with him.

qa.q: How might the neighbour have felt hearing Jeevan's voice?
qa.a: The neighbour, hurt and dazed, might feel a little comforted knowing someone stayed and help was coming.

passage: I'm Swati, and I've never done a first-aid course. But last month, at the college gate, my classmate Reena fainted and hit her head on the pavement. People crowded close. I was so scared I almost ran. Instead, I asked everyone to step back and give her air, and I called 112. The operator asked if she was breathing. She was. "Don't move her. Stay beside her. Tell me if anything changes." So I stayed, kneeling, talking to Reena even though I didn't know if she could hear me. When she opened her eyes, I told her not to get up. The ambulance came. I wasn't brave, exactly. I just did what the voice on the phone said.

qa.q: Where did Reena faint?
qa.a: At the college gate.

qa.q: How did Swati feel when Reena fell?
qa.a: Swati felt so scared that running away was tempting.

qa.q: What did Swati do that helped, even without training?
qa.a: Swati cleared the crowd, called 112, followed the operator, stayed beside Reena and told her not to get up.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt when she opened her eyes?
qa.a: Reena was likely confused and frightened, but reassured to find a friend beside her and help on the way.

grounding: An untrained young adult describes making space, calling emergency services and following the operator's instructions without moving the injured classmate.

passage:
Warden's note, Tuesday night.
At about 9:15 a delivery rider skidded on the wet road outside our gate and lay on his side, groaning. His name, we later learned, was Jatin. Binita, a second-year resident with no first-aid training, was first out of the gate. I could see she was shaking. She still did things in order. She asked our watchman to stand in the road with his torch and slow the cars. She called 112 and put the phone on speaker. When Jatin tried to sit up and pull off his helmet, she knelt beside him and said, "Please stay still, help is coming," because the operator had told her not to move him. She kept talking to him, asked his name, told the operator he was awake and breathing. She stayed until the ambulance took him. Afterwards I sat with her over tea; she cried a little. Tomorrow I'll ask the college about a first-aid session for residents.

qa.q: Who did Binita ask to slow the cars?
qa.a: The watchman, standing in the road with his torch.

qa.q: How was Binita feeling as she helped, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She was frightened, shaking and crying a little afterwards, yet focused enough to do each step in order.

qa.q: Which of Binita's steps protected Jatin most, and why?
qa.a: Keeping him still instead of letting him sit up or take off the helmet, as the operator said, because moving a badly hurt person can make things worse.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Jatin lying on the wet road?
qa.a: He was likely scared and confused, and a calm voice asking his name and saying help was coming would have made him feel less alone.

grounding: Shows an untrained, scared person keeping the scene safe, calling emergency services, staying with the injured rider and following the operator's advice not to move him.
